overview: Security governance is how an organization directs and checks its security work: who decides, which rules apply, how risk is handled and how anyone knows it is working. This domain covers four connected ideas: planning governance, risk and compliance (GRC); keeping the business running through redundancy, business continuity and disaster recovery; building security awareness; and measuring whether security is effective. Each idea now includes how artificial intelligence (AI) changes the picture.
analogy: Think of running a community hospital. The board sets direction and answers for results, department heads own their areas, and staff follow written procedures and the law. Backup generators and a second supply route keep care going when the power fails or a road floods, and regular drills prove the plans work. Every new hire learns to question a stranger asking for patient records. Each month, leaders read a short report on infection rates, wait times and early warnings. Security governance works the same way for information.

topics.overview: Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) joins three jobs that often sit apart: setting direction, managing risk and meeting obligations. Planning GRC well means everyone knows who decides, which rules apply and how the organization proves it follows them. This topic covers why GRC matters, the roles involved, the frameworks it draws on and the tools that support it, including rules for using AI.
can_do: Explain what each part of GRC does and why joining them closes gaps and cuts duplicated work
Match a governance decision to the right role, from the board to the everyday user
Tell a legal or contract obligation from a voluntary framework, and pick a framework for a stated need
Apply risk appetite, tolerance and an AI acceptable use policy to an everyday decision

subtopics.name: GRC Purpose and Importance
subtopics.definition: Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) is a coordinated way to direct an organization, manage its risks and meet its obligations, using shared owners, information and processes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: When the three run in separate silos, teams duplicate work, miss gaps and give leaders conflicting pictures. GRC lines security up with business goals, so decisions rest on one shared view of risk.
how_it_works: Governance sets direction: leaders define goals, assign accountability, approve policy and oversee results.
Risk management finds, rates and treats risks to those goals, within limits that leadership sets.
Compliance confirms the organization meets laws, regulations, contracts and its own policies, and keeps evidence that it does.
All three share one set of records, such as a risk register and a control library, so one control can satisfy several needs.
GRC is a cycle, not a project: plan, act, measure the results and improve.

rows.label: Main question
cells: Who decides, and where are we going?
What could stop us, and what do we do about it?
Are we meeting our obligations, and can we prove it?

rows.label: Led by
cells: Risk owners, supported by security and risk teams
The compliance function, with control owners

subtopics.example: A regional logistics firm keeps its privacy checklist in legal, its risk list in IT and its policies in human resources. A review finds one backup control tested three times, while a contract clause on breach notice has no owner. Leadership creates one GRC program with a shared control list. A junior analyst maps obligations to existing controls and flags the unowned clause to the compliance lead.

review: Confirm each policy, risk and obligation record names an owner
Compare the risk records with the obligations list for gaps
Point out any duplicate work across separate teams
evidence: Shared control library mapped to risks and obligations
Risk register entries with owners and review dates
Compliance calendar showing upcoming reporting deadlines
audit_focus.recommend: Raise any mismatch between risk records and obligations with the GRC program owner for a decision.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management sets GRC direction and approves the program

subtopics.isaca_rule: GRC exists so security serves business goals. When a question asks why GRC matters, choose alignment, clear accountability and one shared view of risk over any single tool or control. A practitioner supports the program by keeping records accurate and flagging gaps to the owner.

exam_traps.trap: GRC is a software product the security team buys and runs.
exam_traps.why: Tools support GRC, but GRC is a management approach: leaders direct, owners manage risk and compliance is proven. A platform without owners changes nothing.

exam_traps.trap: Being compliant means the organization is secure.
exam_traps.why: Compliance shows a set of obligations is met at a point in time. Risks outside those rules, and new threats, can remain. GRC uses risk, not only checklists, to decide what to protect.

key_terms.definition: A team or set of records that works apart from others, so information is not shared.
One list of the organization's controls, each with an owner, mapped to the risks and obligations it addresses.
Making sure security work supports the organization's goals instead of competing with them.

subtopics.name: Planning a GRC Program
subtopics.definition: Planning a governance, risk and compliance (GRC) program means setting its scope, goals, owners, obligations and framework first, so effort goes where risk is greatest.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a plan, a program copies someone else's checklist, protects the wrong things and leaves owners unclear. A plan ties security work to the mission and gives leaders something to approve, fund and measure.
how_it_works: Understand the context: mission, critical services, stakeholders and the risks leaders are willing to take.
List the obligations that apply, such as laws, regulations, contracts and internal policies.
Set the scope, meaning which business units, systems and data are covered, and choose a framework to structure the work.
Assign an owner to each policy, risk and control, and have senior management approve a charter and budget.
Decide up front how success will be measured and reported, then review and adjust the plan on a set cycle.
subtopics.example: A small online bookseller starts taking card payments and selling to customers abroad. Before buying any tools, the owner asks the IT lead to list what now applies: card industry rules, privacy law and the payment provider's contract. They agree the scope covers the shop website, payment data and staff laptops. A new support technician is asked to inventory those laptops so the plan starts from an accurate list.

review: Confirm the scope names every in-scope system and data set
Compare the asset inventory with the scope for missing items
Report anything outside scope that handles sensitive data
evidence: Program charter approved and signed by senior management
Obligations list with an owner for each duty
Asset inventory for the in-scope systems
audit_focus.recommend: Send any system or data set missing from the scope to the program owner to decide on coverage.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management signs off the program before work begins

subtopics.isaca_rule: Plan before you buy. Context and obligations come first, then scope, owners and a framework, then tools. When a stem asks what to do FIRST when building a program, pick the step that understands the business and its duties, not a purchase or a technical fix.

exam_traps.trap: Start a GRC program by buying a platform or running a vulnerability scan.
exam_traps.why: Tools and scans answer how, not what or why. Without known obligations, scope and owners, the tool has nothing to measure against and the scan results have no priority.

exam_traps.trap: Copy a large company's policy set to save time.
exam_traps.why: Obligations, risk appetite and critical services differ by organization. Borrowed policies can miss required duties or demand controls nobody can run.

key_terms.definition: The boundaries of a program: which units, locations, systems and data it covers.
A short approved document stating a program's purpose, authority, scope and leadership sponsor.
A duty the organization must meet, set by law, regulation, contract or its own policy.

subtopics.name: Governance Roles and Accountability
subtopics.definition: Governance roles set out who directs, who owns, who looks after and who uses information, so every decision and duty has a named person behind it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Unclear roles let risky decisions go unmade, or get made by the wrong person. On the exam, many answers turn on who has the authority to approve, accept or change something.
how_it_works: The board oversees the organization and answers for it; it sets direction and risk appetite but does not run daily security.
Senior management approves policy, funds the program and accepts risk on the organization's behalf.
A data owner, usually a business leader, classifies data and decides who may use it; a system owner answers for a system.
A custodian, often IT, carries out the owner's decisions: backups, access changes and patching.
Users follow policy and report problems. Tasks can be delegated, but accountability stays with the owner.

rows.label: Main duty
cells: Decides classification and who gets access
Runs the controls the owner chose

rows.label: Answers for
cells: The data or system and its risk

subtopics.example: At a city council, a payroll clerk asks the help desk to give a new temporary worker access to salary records. The help desk technician notices the request has no approval from the payroll manager, who owns that data. Instead of granting it to be helpful, the technician returns the ticket and asks for the owner's written approval.

review: Match each request's approver against the data inventory
Compare who approved a change with who is allowed to
Escalate decisions that sit outside your authority
evidence: Access tickets showing owner approval before the custodian acted
Data inventory listing an owner for each data set
Policy approval page signed by senior management
audit_focus.recommend: Return any request lacking the right approval to the requester and copy the data owner.
audit_focus.decides: Data owners grant access; senior management signs off policy

subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the decision to the role. Owners decide and accept risk, custodians carry out, users follow and report, and senior management approves policy. An entry-level practitioner who spots a decision outside their authority routes it to the owner instead of making it.

exam_traps.trap: The security analyst who wrote the policy should approve it.
exam_traps.why: Analysts can draft policy, but approval belongs to senior management, which has the authority and the accountability. A policy approved only by its author has no organizational backing.

exam_traps.trap: IT owns the data because IT runs the servers.
exam_traps.why: Running the servers makes IT the custodian. The business leader who relies on the data is the owner and decides classification and access.

key_terms.definition: Being answerable for an outcome; it stays with the owner even when tasks are delegated.
Handing a task to someone else while keeping accountability for the result.
The governing body that oversees management and answers for the organization's direction.
Top executives who approve policy, fund security and accept risk for the organization.

subtopics.name: Compliance Obligations and Evidence
subtopics.definition: Compliance means meeting the requirements that apply to the organization, from laws and regulations to contracts and its own policies, and being able to prove it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Missing an obligation can bring fines, lost contracts, legal action and lost trust. Regulators and customers rarely accept "we do it" without records, so evidence matters as much as the control itself.
how_it_works: Identify each obligation, where it comes from and what it requires, then assign an owner.
Map every obligation to the controls that meet it; one control can cover several obligations.
Collect evidence as work happens: logs, tickets, signed approvals and test results.
Check compliance on a schedule through self-assessments and internal or external audits.
Track each gap as a finding with an owner and a due date until it is fixed.

rows.label: Example
cells: A privacy law such as the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) rules required by a payment provider
A rule that every laptop uses full-disk encryption

rows.label: Optional?
cells: No, for the staff it covers

subtopics.example: A dental practice signs up for a cloud booking service. The contract requires the practice to report any suspected data breach within 48 hours, and health privacy law adds its own deadlines. The office manager adds both duties to the obligations list. When the IT assistant later sees an unusual login to the booking system, they follow the incident procedure at once, knowing the reporting clock may already be running.

review: Confirm each listed obligation has an owner and a mapped control
Compare upcoming deadlines with the compliance calendar
Report missing, late or unsigned evidence to the control owner
evidence: System logs and tickets produced while the control ran
Dated sign-offs from the people who approved each change
Open findings list with owners and due dates
audit_focus.recommend: Tell the control owner as soon as evidence is missing or a deadline is at risk.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management decides how and when a compliance gap is closed

subtopics.isaca_rule: Compliance is proven, not claimed. Know where each obligation comes from, map it to a control and keep the evidence. When a stem describes a legal or contract duty, the right answer meets it on time and leaves a record; a voluntary framework does not replace a legal duty.

exam_traps.trap: Passing last year's audit means the organization is still compliant.
exam_traps.why: Compliance is ongoing. Systems, laws and contracts change, and controls slip. An old audit shows the state at that time, not today.

exam_traps.trap: Following a respected framework satisfies every legal requirement.
exam_traps.why: Frameworks are voluntary guidance. Laws and contracts can demand specific things, such as breach notice deadlines, that a framework does not mention.

key_terms.definition: Records that show a control operated, such as logs, tickets, approvals or test results.
An independent, structured check, based on evidence, of whether requirements are met.
A documented gap between a requirement and what actually happens, with an owner and a fix date.
A government body that sets and enforces rules for an industry.

subtopics.name: GRC Frameworks
subtopics.definition: A governance, risk and compliance (GRC) framework is a published structure of practices and controls an organization adopts to organize and measure its security work.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Frameworks save organizations from inventing security from scratch and give leaders, auditors and partners a common language. Choosing one that fits the need makes progress easier to plan, compare and report.
how_it_works: Most frameworks are voluntary; an organization adopts one by choice, or because a contract or regulator requires it.
Some describe outcomes to reach, some list specific controls, and some define a management system that can be certified.
Organizations often combine them: one for the overall structure and another for detailed controls.
A crosswalk maps one framework's items to another's, so one control can show progress against both.
Adopting a framework includes tailoring it: keep what fits the risks and record why anything is left out.

types.meaning: Outcome-based structure with six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Govern was added in the 2024 release.
International standard for an information security management system (ISMS); organizations can be certified against it.
A seven-step process for system risk in NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2: prepare, categorize, select, implement, assess, authorize and monitor.
A prioritized set of 18 controls, with Implementation Groups that show smaller organizations where to start.

types.term: NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
types.meaning: Voluntary guidance for managing AI risk, built on four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.
International standard for a business continuity management system; organizations can be certified against it.

subtopics.example: A mid-sized school district wants to show its board progress on security. The IT director adopts the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 for reporting by function and uses the CIS Controls to choose concrete first steps. A newly hired technician is asked to record, for each safeguard they configure, which CSF outcome it supports, so the progress report stays accurate.

review: Confirm which framework and version the organization has adopted
Map each safeguard you configure to the framework item it supports
Report framework items marked out of scope without a reason
evidence: Framework profile or ISO statement of applicability listing chosen controls
Crosswalk mapping internal controls to framework items
Quarterly status report grouped by CSF function
audit_focus.recommend: Send unexplained exclusions or stale mappings to the GRC lead so they can be reviewed and recorded.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management chooses the framework and approves tailoring decisions

subtopics.isaca_rule: Pick the framework that fits the stated need: an outcome structure for board reporting, a control list for practical first steps, a certifiable standard when customers want proof. Frameworks guide; laws and contracts require. Tailoring is expected, but leaving something out needs a recorded reason.

exam_traps.trap: A framework must be adopted in full, every item, or it is not really being followed.
exam_traps.why: Frameworks expect tailoring to an organization's risks and size. What matters is a documented, reasoned choice of what applies, not blind adoption of every item.

exam_traps.trap: NIST CSF 2.0 is a certification an organization can be audited and certified against.
exam_traps.why: The CSF is voluntary guidance with no certification scheme. ISO/IEC 27001 is the common certifiable standard for an information security management system.

key_terms.definition: A mapping that shows how items in one framework or standard match items in another.
Adjusting a framework or control set to fit an organization's risks, size and duties, with the reasons recorded.
Formal confirmation by an accredited body that a management system meets a standard's requirements.

subtopics.name: GRC Tools and Automation
subtopics.definition: Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) tools are software platforms that keep risks, controls, policies and evidence in one place and automate routine tasks such as reminders.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Spreadsheets and email chains break as programs grow: versions conflict, evidence goes missing and deadlines slip. A tool gives one current record, but only if owners keep it accurate and act on what it shows.
how_it_works: A risk register module records each risk with its owner, rating, treatment and review date.
A control library links each control to the risks and obligations it covers.
Policy management tracks versions, approvals, review dates and staff acknowledgments.
Automated evidence collection pulls data from systems, such as configuration settings or access lists, on a schedule.
Monitoring rules flag a control that drifts from its expected state, such as disk encryption switched off.
Dashboards and reports turn the stored data into views for each audience.
subtopics.example: A nonprofit health clinic moves its policies and risk list into a GRC platform. Each night the platform pulls laptop settings, and one morning it flags a laptop with disk encryption off. The alert goes to a junior IT technician, who confirms the setting on the device, opens a change ticket and records the fix in the platform.

review: Confirm the alert reflects a real gap before acting
Compare the tool's record with the live system setting
Link the corrected setting to its change record
evidence: Platform alert history showing when the control drifted
Configuration export taken after the fix
Signed read-and-accept records for current policies
audit_focus.recommend: Pass alerts outside your permissions to the control owner instead of changing the monitoring rule yourself.
audit_focus.decides: The control owner decides how a monitored control is set

subtopics.isaca_rule: A tool supports governance but never replaces it: owners, decisions and follow-up still come from people. When a tool raises an alert or a gap, the practitioner's job is to confirm it, act within the procedure and leave a record, not to silence the alert.

exam_traps.trap: Once the GRC platform is installed, compliance is automatic.
exam_traps.why: Tools collect and display data. People still decide risk treatment, approve policies and fix gaps. Unowned alerts are just a well-organized list of problems.

exam_traps.trap: Turn off a noisy monitoring alert so the dashboard shows green.
exam_traps.why: Hiding an alert hides the risk. Confirm whether it is a real gap or a false alarm, then fix it or ask the control owner to adjust the rule, with a record.

key_terms.definition: Automated, frequent checks that a control is still in its expected state, with alerts when it drifts.
A recorded statement that a person has read a policy or that a control is in place.
One agreed, current record that everyone uses instead of separate copies.

subtopics.name: Risk Appetite, Tolerance and the Risk Register
subtopics.definition: Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk leaders will take to reach their goals; risk tolerance sets specific, measurable limits within that appetite.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Appetite and tolerance turn "be secure" into decisions people can act on. They tell a team when a risk is acceptable, when it must be treated and when it must go to a leader.
how_it_works: The board and senior management set risk appetite, usually as broad statements for each kind of risk.
Tolerances turn appetite into specific limits, such as no more than four hours of downtime for patient records.
Each risk goes into the risk register with an owner, a rating and a chosen treatment.
The usual treatments are avoid, reduce (mitigate), transfer (share) and accept.
Only someone with authority, usually the risk owner or senior management, may formally accept a risk.
Accepted risks carry a reason and a review date, because conditions change.

rows.label: Level
cells: Specific to one objective or risk

rows.label: Set by
cells: Senior management and risk owners, within the appetite

rows.label: Example
cells: "We take very little risk with customer data"
"No more than 1% of laptops unencrypted at any time"

subtopics.example: A small accounting firm's leaders state a very low appetite for exposing client data. A help desk technician finds an old file-sharing link, open to anyone who has the address, that holds client tax files. The technician does not decide the risk is fine because the link is hard to guess. They disable the link, as the procedure allows, and log a risk register entry for the data owner.

review: Compare a newly found risk with the stated tolerance
Confirm the register entry names an owner and a review date
Note the data involved, the exposure and possible fixes
evidence: Risk appetite statement approved by senior leadership
Register history showing who changed a rating, and when
Signed risk acceptance with a reason and an expiry date
audit_focus.recommend: Log the risk and send it to the risk owner with the facts they need to decide.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner or senior management decides treatment and acceptance

subtopics.isaca_rule: Leaders set appetite, owners accept risk, and practitioners never accept risk on the organization's behalf. When a stem shows a risk above the stated tolerance, the right move is to treat or escalate it to the owner with a record, not to quietly live with it.

exam_traps.trap: The analyst who found a risk can accept it if the fix costs too much.
exam_traps.why: Accepting risk needs authority. The analyst documents the risk and the cost of fixing it; the risk owner or senior management decides.

exam_traps.trap: An accepted risk is closed for good.
exam_traps.why: Acceptance holds only while conditions hold. Threats, systems and business value change, so every accepted risk carries a review date.

key_terms.definition: A central list of identified risks, each with an owner, rating, chosen treatment and review date.
The person accountable for managing a particular risk, including deciding how it is treated.
Risk left after controls are applied; it must sit within tolerance or be formally accepted.

subtopics.name: Governing AI Use
subtopics.definition: Governing the use of artificial intelligence (AI) means setting rules for which AI tools staff may use, for what tasks and with which data.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Staff adopt AI assistants faster than policies appear. Pasting confidential data into an unapproved public tool can leak it, breach contracts or privacy law, and leave no record of where it went.
how_it_works: An AI acceptable use policy, approved by senior management, says which tools are allowed and for what purposes.
An approved tools list names vetted services, often business versions whose contracts limit data use.
Data rules follow classification: for example, no confidential or personal data in public AI tools.
An AI inventory records where AI is used, who owns each use and what data it touches.
People check AI output before relying on it, especially for decisions affecting customers or safety.
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 can help structure this governance.
subtopics.example: A marketing assistant at a regional bank wants a free online chatbot to summarize customer complaints that include names and account numbers. Bank policy allows only the approved business assistant, and only for data classified internal or lower. The assistant removes the personal details, uses the approved tool and asks the data owner whether the full file may ever be used.

review: Confirm a tool is on the approved list before using it
Look up the data's classification label before pasting anything
Note colleagues' use of tools missing from the approved list
evidence: Vendor terms showing how each approved service handles prompts
Signed staff acknowledgment of the AI acceptable use policy
AI inventory entries naming an owner for each use
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected shadow AI to the security team rather than blocking or approving tools on your own.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management approves the AI policy; data owners decide data use

subtopics.isaca_rule: Use only approved AI tools, for approved purposes, with data the policy allows. If unsure whether data may go into an AI tool, treat it as not allowed and ask the data owner. Unapproved tools are a policy issue to report, not a shortcut to take.

exam_traps.trap: A public AI chatbot is fine for work data as long as you delete the chat afterward.
exam_traps.why: Deleting your copy doesn't prove the provider deleted the data or kept it out of training. Only approved tools under agreed terms may handle work data.

exam_traps.trap: Ban every AI tool so the risk disappears.
exam_traps.why: Blanket bans often push staff toward hidden, unapproved tools. Governance works better with approved options, clear data rules and monitoring.

key_terms.definition: A policy stating what staff may and may not do with the organization's systems and data.
AI tools used for work without the organization's approval.
A list of where AI is used, who owns each use and what data it touches.

topics.overview: Redundancy keeps services running when a part fails, and continuity and recovery plans cover the failures redundancy can't absorb. This topic covers business continuity (BC) and disaster recovery (DR), the business impact analysis (BIA) and recovery targets behind them, backups, recovery sites, plan testing, and what changes when services depend on AI.
can_do: Tell business continuity from disaster recovery, and redundancy from backup
Use the recovery time objective (RTO), recovery point objective (RPO) and maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) to judge a backup schedule or recovery site
Put the five plan test types in order from least to most disruptive
Explain why AI models, settings and datasets need backups, and why model drift is a continuity risk

subtopics.name: Redundancy and High Availability
subtopics.definition: Redundancy means having spare components, paths or copies ready to take over when one fails, so a single failure does not stop a service.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Hardware breaks, power drops and cables get cut. Removing single points of failure keeps critical services available, the "A" in the confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA) triad.
how_it_works: Start by finding single points of failure: one server, one power feed, one internet link or one key person.
Add a spare for each critical one, such as a second power supply, network link or server.
Failover moves work to the spare, automatically or by a set procedure, when the primary fails.
High availability designs combine redundancy and failover so users notice little or no outage.
Place spares in another building or region when a whole site could be lost.
Redundancy copies mistakes instantly, so it does not replace backups.

types.meaning: A redundant array of independent disks (RAID) that writes the same data to two disks; either disk can fail without data loss.
Spreads data and recovery information across three or more disks; survives the loss of any one disk.
Several servers work as one; if one fails, another takes over its work.
Spreads requests across several servers, so losing one reduces capacity instead of stopping service.
An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) bridges short outages with batteries; a generator covers longer ones.
Two internet providers or paths, so one cut cable does not cut the service.

subtopics.example: A small warehouse runs its order system on one server with one internet line. After a storm cuts the line for a day, the operations manager approves a second line from a different provider and a standby server that takes over automatically. A junior technician is asked to test the switch-over every month and log each result for the manager to review.

review: Confirm the spare actually takes over during a scheduled test
Compare power and network diagrams against known single points of failure
Report any critical service that still depends on one component
evidence: Failover test log with dates, duration and outcome
Monitoring alerts showing when the standby took over
Current diagram of power, network and server paths
audit_focus.recommend: Log any untested or missing spare and pass it to the system owner for a decision.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner decides which redundancy to fund

subtopics.isaca_rule: Redundancy protects availability against component failure; backups protect against loss and corruption. When a stem describes one part whose failure stops everything, remove the single point of failure. When it describes deleted, corrupted or encrypted data, redundancy is not the fix.

exam_traps.trap: RAID or a mirrored server means we don't need backups.
exam_traps.why: Mirroring copies every change, including accidental deletion, corruption and ransomware encryption. Only a separate, earlier copy lets you go back to good data.

exam_traps.trap: Two servers in the same rack give full protection.
exam_traps.why: Both share the same power, room and building, so a fire, flood or power cut takes out both. Distance between copies matters for site-wide events.

key_terms.definition: One component whose failure stops a whole service because nothing can take its place.
Switching work from a failed component to its standby.
A design goal of keeping a service running with very little downtime, using redundancy and failover.

subtopics.name: Business Continuity vs Disaster Recovery
subtopics.definition: Business continuity (BC) keeps critical business functions running during a disruption; disaster recovery (DR) restores the technology and data those functions depend on.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Restored servers are useless if staff have nowhere to work, no one can reach customers or payroll can't run. Treating DR as the whole of BC leaves people, places and processes unplanned.
how_it_works: The BC plan covers the whole business: people, facilities, suppliers, communications and manual workarounds.
The DR plan is the technical part: restoring systems, networks and data, often at an alternate site.
Both start from the business impact analysis (BIA), which sets priorities and recovery targets.
Plans name who may declare a disaster, how staff are contacted and who speaks to the public.
Human safety comes first in every plan: evacuate and account for people before saving equipment or data.
Plans end with a controlled return to normal operations, at the main site or a replacement.

rows.label: Main goal
cells: Detect, contain and recover from a security incident

rows.label: Typical trigger
cells: Any major disruption: fire, pandemic, supplier failure
Loss of a data center, system or data
A security event that harms or threatens assets

rows.label: Example action
cells: Staff work from a second office
Restore servers at a recovery site

subtopics.example: A flood closes a call center's building overnight. The IT team restores the phone and ticket systems in the cloud within hours, which is disaster recovery. But no one had planned where the agents would sit, how they would get laptops or who would update customers. A support analyst on the morning shift follows the call tree, checks in with their team lead and waits for instructions instead of driving to the closed site.

review: Confirm your contact details in the call tree are current
Compare the plan's role list with current staff and deputies
Report plan sections that cover systems but not people
evidence: Call tree with phone numbers tested in the last exercise
Approved plan showing who may activate it
Results and actions from the last plan review
audit_focus.recommend: Send outdated contacts or missing roles to the business continuity manager before the next test.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management or a named crisis lead declares a disaster

subtopics.isaca_rule: DR is one part of BC, not all of it. When a stem asks about keeping the business running, think people, places, suppliers and communication as well as systems. Whatever the scenario, people's safety comes before any asset.

exam_traps.trap: Our disaster recovery plan is our business continuity plan.
exam_traps.why: DR restores technology. BC also covers staff, workspace, suppliers, manual workarounds and communication. A full system restore with no one able to work is not continuity.

exam_traps.trap: During a fire, grab the backup drives on the way out.
exam_traps.why: Life safety comes first. Plans keep backups offsite precisely so no one has to risk injury to save data.

key_terms.definition: A set list of who contacts whom, in order, to alert staff during a disruption.
The formal decision by an authorized person to activate the recovery plan.
Moving operations from the alternate site back to the restored main site in a controlled way.

subtopics.name: Business Impact Analysis (BIA)
subtopics.definition: A business impact analysis (BIA) identifies an organization's critical functions, what each depends on and how harm grows over time if each one stops.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The BIA decides what is recovered first and how fast. Every later choice, from backup frequency to recovery site, rests on it, so a weak BIA spreads errors into every plan.
how_it_works: List business functions, such as taking orders or paying staff, before listing systems.
Ask function owners to rate financial, legal, safety, customer and reputation harm at several outage lengths.
Record what each function depends on: systems, data, people, sites and suppliers.
Set recovery targets for each critical function, starting with its maximum tolerable downtime (MTD).
Rank functions so the most critical are restored first.
Senior management approves the results, and the BIA is updated when the business changes.

rows.label: Main question
cells: If this function stops, how bad is it over time?
What could go wrong, and how likely is it?

subtopics.example: A university's BIA team asks the registrar how long course enrollment can stop during the first week of term. The answer is a few hours, while the alumni newsletter can wait a month. Enrollment depends on the student system, the sign-in service and an outside payment provider. A help desk analyst assisting with the survey adds the payment provider to the dependency list after a staff member mentions it.

review: Confirm each critical function lists every dependency, suppliers included
Compare BIA priorities with the order of steps in the recovery plan
Report functions or suppliers the BIA has missed
evidence: Owner-confirmed impact ratings at several outage lengths
Dependency list matched to the asset and supplier lists
Signed approval page for the current BIA
audit_focus.recommend: Pass missing functions or dependencies to the business continuity manager to add at the next update.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management signs off which functions recover first

subtopics.isaca_rule: The BIA starts from business functions and their owners, not from IT's server list. Owners say what hurts and how fast; senior management approves the priorities. When a stem asks what must come before choosing recovery sites or backup schedules, the answer is the BIA.

exam_traps.trap: Begin the BIA by rating how important each server is.
exam_traps.why: Servers matter only because functions depend on them. Starting from servers misses manual steps, people and suppliers, and ranks technology instead of business harm.

exam_traps.trap: The BIA is mainly about how likely each disaster is.
exam_traps.why: The BIA measures impact over time. Likelihood belongs to the risk assessment, and a rare event can still have an impact that demands planning.

key_terms.definition: A business activity whose loss would quickly cause serious harm, so it is restored first.
Anything a function needs to run, such as a system, data set, person, site or supplier.
The business leader responsible for a function, who supplies and confirms its BIA ratings.

subtopics.name: Recovery Objectives: MTD, RTO and RPO
subtopics.definition: Recovery objectives are limits set by the business: how long a function can be down and how much recent data it can afford to lose.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These numbers drive cost. A shorter downtime target needs a readier site; a smaller data-loss target needs more frequent copies. Confusing them leads to buying the wrong fix.
how_it_works: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) is the longest a function can be out before harm becomes unacceptable.
Recovery time objective (RTO) is the target time to bring the function back; it must fit within the MTD.
Recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, the business can lose; it looks back from the disruption.
RPO drives how often data is copied; RTO drives how ready the recovery site and team must be.
Business owners set these targets in the business impact analysis (BIA); IT designs solutions to meet them.

rows.label: Question it answers
cells: How long before the outage is intolerable?
How fast must we be running again?
How much recent data can we lose?

rows.label: Direction
cells: Backward to the last good copy

rows.label: What meets it
cells: Not met directly; the RTO must fit inside it
Recovery site, staff and tested procedures

The practice manager says losing more than one hour of appointments would be serious, and the system must be back within four hours. A junior technician notices the nightly backup leaves up to 24 hours of bookings at risk, beyond the one-hour RPO, and reports the gap to the IT lead.

review: Line up actual copy times against each data-loss target
Time a test restore and compare it with the downtime target
Report any target the current setup cannot meet
evidence: Backup job logs showing when copies actually ran
Timed restore test results for each critical system
BIA record with owner-approved MTD, RTO and RPO
audit_focus.recommend: Report missed targets to the system owner with the numbers, rather than changing the schedule or the target yourself.
audit_focus.decides: Business owners set the targets; senior management funds any gap

subtopics.isaca_rule: RPO is about data, looking back; RTO is about time, looking forward; MTD is the outer limit the RTO must fit inside. A hot site shortens downtime but does nothing for data loss, while more frequent backups shrink data loss but do not speed recovery.

exam_traps.trap: A faster recovery site will reduce how much data we lose.
exam_traps.why: Site readiness affects the RTO. Data loss depends on when the last good copy was made, so only more frequent backups or replication improve the RPO.

exam_traps.trap: IT should set the RTO to whatever current systems can achieve.
exam_traps.why: Targets come from business impact in the BIA. If IT can't meet one, that is a gap to report and fund, not a reason to loosen it.

key_terms.definition: Time after systems return to check data and clear backlog; RTO plus WRT must fit inside the MTD.
Copying data to another location continuously or near continuously, which supports a very small RPO.
Another name for MTD, used in many continuity standards.

subtopics.memory_aid: RPO: the Point you roll back to. RTO: the Time until you are running. MTD: the hard limit.

subtopics.name: Backups: Types, the 3-2-1 Rule and Restore Testing
subtopics.definition: A backup is a separate copy of data, and often of system settings, kept so the original can be restored after loss, corruption or attack.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Backups are the last defense against ransomware, mistakes and hardware loss. A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a control, and one that attackers can reach may be encrypted too.
how_it_works: Choose the backup type and frequency to meet the recovery point objective (RPO).
Follow the 3-2-1 rule: three copies of data, on two different types of storage, with one copy offsite.
Keep at least one copy offline or immutable, so ransomware or a stolen admin account can't change it.
Protect backups like the original: encrypt them and limit who can delete them.
Test restores on a schedule and time them against the recovery time objective (RTO).

types.meaning: Copies all selected data every time. Slowest to make and simplest to restore: one set.
Copies only what changed since the last backup of any kind. Fast to make; a restore needs the last full plus every incremental since, in order.
Copies everything changed since the last full backup. Grows each day; a restore needs the last full plus only the latest differential.
A quick point-in-time image of a system or volume. Useful, but often stored on the same system, so not a backup on its own.
