subtopics.example: A law office backs up its file server every night to a disk in the same closet, and the copies have never been restored. A paralegal's laptop picks up ransomware that spreads to the server and encrypts the backup disk too. After recovering, the office adds an immutable cloud copy, and a new IT assistant gets a monthly task: restore a sample folder and record how long it took.

review: Restore a sample of files and time the result
Confirm one copy sits beyond reach of everyday admin logins
Compare the list of backed-up systems with the asset inventory
evidence: Restore test record with date, data restored and time taken
Backup job reports showing completed and failed jobs
Storage settings showing retention lock or immutability
audit_focus.recommend: Report failed restores or unprotected backup copies to the system owner the same day.
audit_focus.decides: The system owner decides backup scope and retention, within policy

subtopics.isaca_rule: A backup counts only if it can be restored in time and an attacker can't reach it. When a stem lists backup choices, look for separation (offsite, offline or immutable) and proven restores. Faster backups don't help if nobody has ever tested getting the data back.

exam_traps.trap: Backups run every night with no errors, so recovery is assured.
exam_traps.why: A successful job only shows data was copied. Corrupt files, missing systems or a slow restore show up only when you actually restore and time it.

exam_traps.trap: An incremental restore needs only the full and the latest incremental.
exam_traps.why: That is the differential rule. Each incremental holds only the changes since the backup before it, so a restore needs the full plus every incremental, in order.

key_terms.definition: A backup that can't be changed or deleted, even by an administrator, until a set retention period ends.
A copy disconnected from networks, sometimes called air-gapped, so remote attackers can't reach it.
How long each backup is kept before it may be deleted.

subtopics.name: Recovery Sites
subtopics.definition: A recovery site is an alternate place to run critical systems or work when the main site is unusable, ranging from an empty room to a fully running copy.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The site must match the recovery time objective (RTO). Too slow, and the business misses its targets; too ready, and money goes on standby equipment the business didn't need.
how_it_works: Readier sites recover faster and cost more to keep ready.
Match the site to the RTO from the business impact analysis (BIA), not to habit or budget alone.
Keep the site far enough away that one regional event, such as a flood, can't hit both sites.
Cloud recovery usually means paying for stored copies day to day and for computing power mainly during a failover or test.
Contracts and regular tests confirm the site will be ready, and big enough, when needed.

rows.label: What is ready
cells: Equipment and connections; data must be restored
Stored copies; computing started on demand

rows.label: Typical recovery time
cells: Minutes to hours, if built and tested

rows.label: Fits an RTO of
cells: About a day to a few days

subtopics.example: An online pharmacy's BIA sets a four-hour RTO for order processing. To save money, the finance team proposes a cold site across town. A junior analyst preparing the comparison notes two problems: a cold site would take days to equip, and across town sits in the same flood zone. They flag both points to the continuity manager before the decision meeting.

review: Compare each site option's recovery time with the RTO
Confirm the site sits outside the main site's regional hazards
Report any recovery site that has not been tested recently
evidence: Latest failover test record with time to full operation
Recovery site or provider contract stating capacity and readiness
BIA record showing the RTO for each critical system
audit_focus.recommend: Present site options against the RTO to the continuity manager, flagging any that cannot meet it.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management chooses and funds the recovery site

subtopics.isaca_rule: Let the RTO pick the site: hours means hot or a tested cloud setup, days means warm, weeks means cold. Cost matters, but a cheaper site that misses the RTO isn't a saving. Distance protects against regional events.

exam_traps.trap: A cold site is fine for a system with a four-hour RTO, because it is cheaper.
exam_traps.why: A cold site has no equipment or data, so getting it running takes days or weeks. It can't meet an RTO measured in hours.

exam_traps.trap: Moving to the cloud means recovery is automatic.
exam_traps.why: Cloud recovery still needs copies in another region, tested procedures and enough capacity. A cloud region can fail too, and the customer stays responsible for its own data and settings.

key_terms.definition: A trailer or container with equipment that can be driven to where it is needed.
A deal where two organizations agree to host each other's work in a disaster; cheap but hard to rely on.
A provider service that copies systems to its cloud and runs them there during a disaster.

subtopics.name: Testing and Maintaining BC and DR Plans
subtopics.definition: Plan testing checks that continuity and recovery plans work and that people know their roles, using exercises that range from a document review to a real shutdown.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An untested plan fails at the worst moment: phone numbers are wrong, steps are missing and restores are slower than promised. Testing finds these problems while they are cheap to fix.
how_it_works: Start with low-risk tests and move to more realistic ones as the plan matures.
Set goals for each test, such as meeting the recovery time objective (RTO), and record what happened.
Hold a lessons-learned review after every test and every real event.
Update the plan after tests and after changes to staff, systems, suppliers or sites.
Senior management approves the more disruptive tests, because they put live operations at risk.

types.meaning: Each team reviews the plan on its own for errors and outdated details. No disruption.
Team members meet and talk through a scenario step by step. No systems are touched.
Teams act out their roles in a realistic scenario, sometimes on test systems, without stopping production.
Systems are brought up at the recovery site and run alongside production, which keeps running.
Production is shut down and the business runs from the recovery site. Most realistic and highest risk.

subtopics.example: A food bank's IT volunteers have a disaster recovery (DR) plan nobody has used. Their first test is a tabletop: the director reads out a ransomware scenario, and each person says what they would do. They discover the only person who knows the backup password is on leave. A volunteer records the gap, and the plan owner adds a second key holder before scheduling a parallel test.

review: Confirm your role and contact details before each test
Note every step that failed or ran late during the test
Compare results with the recovery targets the test aimed to meet
evidence: Test report with goals, timings and issues found
Lessons-learned action list with owners and due dates
Plan version history showing updates after each test
audit_focus.recommend: Send test gaps to the plan owner and track them until the plan is updated.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management decides whether production may be shut down

subtopics.isaca_rule: Test in order of risk: checklist, tabletop, simulation, parallel, full interruption. Pick the least disruptive test that meets the goal, and run a full interruption only with senior management approval. A plan stays current only if it is updated after every test and every major change.

exam_traps.trap: The best first test of a new plan is a full interruption, because it is most realistic.
exam_traps.why: A full interruption can cause the very outage the plan is meant to handle. Find basic errors first with checklists and tabletops, then build up to riskier tests.

exam_traps.trap: A parallel test shuts down production to prove the recovery site works.
exam_traps.why: In a parallel test, production keeps running while the recovery site runs alongside it. Shutting production down is a full interruption test.

key_terms.definition: A review after a test or event that records what worked, what didn't and who will fix each gap.
A planned activity where people practice their roles in a plan against a scenario.
Regular updates that keep a plan in step with changes in staff, systems, suppliers and sites.

subtopics.name: Backing Up AI Systems and Model Drift
subtopics.definition: Resilience for artificial intelligence (AI) services means being able to restore the models, settings and data behind them, and noticing when their performance declines.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An AI service can fail even while its servers are up: the model may be lost, misconfigured or slowly getting worse. If a business process depends on it, that is a continuity risk.
how_it_works: Back up more than data: model files and versions, settings, prompts, and training and test datasets.
Keep these backups versioned, so a known-good model and its settings can be restored together.
Model drift is a gradual drop in accuracy as real-world data moves away from the data the model learned from.
Watch for drift with regular performance checks against agreed thresholds, with alerts to the model owner.
Plan a fallback, such as an earlier model version or a manual process, in case the AI service must be paused.
Note dependencies on outside AI providers, whose changes or outages affect the service.
subtopics.example: A delivery firm uses an AI model to predict late parcels, and dispatchers plan routes around it. After the firm adds a new region, accuracy slips week by week. A junior operations analyst sees the weekly accuracy figure fall below the agreed threshold and reports it to the model owner, who switches dispatch to the previous model version while the data is reviewed.

review: Confirm the AI backup set includes the model, settings, prompts and data
Compare the latest accuracy check with the agreed threshold
Tell the model owner about gaps in the backup set
evidence: Versioned backup records for model files and settings
Performance monitoring history with threshold alerts
Documented fallback procedure for the AI service
audit_focus.recommend: Report drift alerts to the model owner with the figures and dates, rather than retraining the model yourself.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides whether to roll back, retrain or pause

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat an AI service like any critical system: know its dependencies, back up everything needed to rebuild it and plan a fallback. Model drift is a continuity risk, because a model can fail slowly while every server looks healthy.

exam_traps.trap: Backing up the training data is enough to recover an AI service.
exam_traps.why: Without the exact model version, settings and prompts, you may not rebuild the same behavior, and retraining from data alone can take days.

exam_traps.trap: If the AI servers are up, the AI service is available.
exam_traps.why: Availability means the service works as needed. A drifting model that gives wrong answers is effectively down for the process that relies on it.

key_terms.definition: A decline in an AI model's accuracy over time as real-world data or conditions change from what it learned.
Returning a system to an earlier, known-good version after a problem.
The person accountable for an AI model's purpose, performance and approved changes.

subtopics.name: AI-Assisted Detection and Playbook Triage
subtopics.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) assisted detection uses learned patterns to spot unusual activity early, while playbooks guide staff through the first triage steps for each alert.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Early detection keeps an incident from growing into a disaster that needs the full recovery plan. Attackers automate too, so playbooks must cover machine-driven attacks as well as human ones.
how_it_works: AI tools learn what normal activity looks like and flag departures, such as a sign-in at an odd hour from a new country.
They can sort and group alerts, so analysts see the most urgent first.
A playbook lists the steps for an alert type: what to check, what to contain and whom to tell.
Playbooks now include automated threats, such as bot-driven password guessing or waves of AI-written phishing.
People stay in the loop: an analyst confirms high-impact alerts before major action and escalates per the playbook.
AI tools make mistakes: false positives waste time, and false negatives miss real attacks.
subtopics.example: At a hospital, an AI monitoring tool flags a nurse's account downloading thousands of patient records at 3 a.m. The playbook tells the night-shift security analyst to confirm the activity in the logs and call the on-call incident lead before any step that could block patient care. The analyst follows it instead of waiting for the day team.

review: Open the playbook written for this kind of alert
Compare the AI alert with the raw logs before escalating
Record each step taken, with times, as the playbook requires
evidence: Alert record with the AI score and supporting log entries
Completed playbook checklist with times and actions
Escalation record showing who was told and when
audit_focus.recommend: Escalate confirmed or unclear high-impact alerts to the incident response team as the playbook directs.
audit_focus.decides: The incident lead decides containment that affects business operations

subtopics.isaca_rule: AI helps you see sooner, but people decide. Follow the playbook for the alert type, confirm before major action and escalate as it directs. An AI score is a lead to check, not proof, and a quiet tool is not proof of safety.

exam_traps.trap: If the AI tool rates an alert low, close it without looking.
exam_traps.why: AI tools miss things and can be fooled. A low score may still need a check under the playbook, especially when other signs agree.

exam_traps.trap: Skip the playbook during a fast attack and improvise to save time.
exam_traps.why: Playbooks exist for speed and consistency under pressure. Making it up risks lost evidence, wrong containment and acting outside your authority.

key_terms.definition: A written set of steps for handling a specific type of alert or incident.
Quickly sorting alerts or incidents by urgency to decide what to handle first.
An alert that flags harmless activity as a threat.
A real threat that a tool fails to flag.

topics.overview: Most attacks reach people before they reach systems. This topic covers building a culture where security matters and leaders model it, and the core ideas every staff member needs: social engineering, phishing, including AI-generated lures, and protecting passwords. A safe, fast reporting habit ties it all together.
can_do: Explain how leadership and a no-blame reporting culture make awareness work
Tell awareness, training and education apart and match each to an audience
Spot the pressure tactics in a social engineering or phishing scenario, including AI-generated lures
Apply current password guidance: length, unique passphrases, a password manager and multifactor authentication (MFA)

subtopics.name: Security Culture and Leadership
subtopics.definition: Security culture is the shared attitudes and habits that shape how people treat security day to day, especially when no one is watching.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Controls fail when people work around them. A culture where staff value security, and feel safe reporting mistakes, catches problems early and makes every other control work better.
how_it_works: Leaders set the tone: they follow the same rules, talk about security and fund it.
Security is framed as part of everyone's job, not only the security team's.
Reporting is easy and safe: one button or contact, with thanks instead of blame for honest mistakes.
Security champions in each team answer questions and pass concerns to the security team.
Culture is judged by behavior, such as reporting rates and survey results, not just course completion.
subtopics.example: A finance director at a manufacturing company insists on skipping multifactor authentication because it slows them down. Staff notice, and soon several others ask for the same exception. The new security analyst neither argues with the director nor quietly grants exceptions. They record each request and send them to the security manager, who raises the pattern with senior management.

review: Follow the same security rules you ask others to follow
Record exception requests instead of granting them informally
Report repeated workarounds to the security manager as a culture signal
evidence: Exception register with approver, reason and expiry date
Staff survey results on willingness to report
Trend in reported incidents and suspected phishing
audit_focus.recommend: Route every exception request, including those from senior leaders, through the documented process to the security manager.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management approves policy exceptions and accepts their risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Culture starts at the top and grows through safe reporting. When a stem asks what MOST improves awareness, prefer leadership support and a no-blame reporting process over more technology or punishment. A practitioner models good habits and routes leaders' exception requests through the proper process.

exam_traps.trap: Punishing staff who click phishing links will improve security.
exam_traps.why: Fear of punishment makes people hide mistakes, and hidden incidents grow. A no-blame culture gets fast reports, which matter more than any single click.

exam_traps.trap: Security culture is the security team's job.
exam_traps.why: The security team supports it, but culture comes from leaders and everyday behavior across the organization. Without leadership backing, awareness efforts fade.

key_terms.definition: The example leaders set through their own behavior and priorities, which staff tend to follow.
A staff member outside the security team who promotes good practice and passes concerns to security.
An approach that treats honest mistakes as chances to learn, while still addressing reckless or deliberate misconduct.

subtopics.name: Awareness, Training and Education
subtopics.definition: Awareness keeps security in mind for everyone, training builds job-specific skills for particular roles, and education builds deeper understanding for those whose careers need it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: One course for everyone wastes time and misses real risks. A developer, a payroll clerk and a help desk agent face different attacks and make different decisions, so they need different learning.
how_it_works: Awareness reaches everyone through short, frequent messages: posters, newsletters, reminders and brief campaigns.
Basic security training happens at onboarding and then on a regular cycle, such as yearly.
Role-based training adds what a job needs: secure coding for developers, caller checks for help desk staff.
Education, such as degrees and certifications, builds deeper knowledge and is usually optional.
Content is refreshed as threats change, for example to cover scams written with artificial intelligence (AI).
NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 (2024) brings all of these together in one cybersecurity and privacy learning program.

rows.label: Example
cells: Help desk staff practice verifying callers

subtopics.example: A hospital gives every staff member the same yearly video. After an attacker talks a help desk agent into resetting a surgeon's password over the phone, the training lead adds a caller-verification module for help desk staff and short monthly reminders for everyone. A help desk technician who completes the module now calls back on the directory number before any reset.

review: Confirm you completed the training your role requires
Compare the mistakes you see with what training covers
Suggest new scam topics to the training lead
evidence: Training records by role, with completion dates
Role-to-course mapping showing who needs which module
Incident trends that point to a training gap
audit_focus.recommend: Pass patterns of repeated mistakes to the training lead so role-based content can be added.
audit_focus.decides: Management sets the training each role requires

subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the learning to the role and the risk. Everyone gets awareness; people with higher-risk duties get role-based training on top. When a stem shows a specific group making a specific mistake, the answer is targeted training for that group, not more of the same general course.

exam_traps.trap: Give everyone the same annual course so training is fair and consistent.
exam_traps.why: The same course is not fair when risks differ. Everyone needs the basics, but roles that handle money, access or code need training on the attacks they actually face.

exam_traps.trap: A completed course means staff will behave securely.
exam_traps.why: Completion shows attendance, not behavior. Judge behavior with measures such as phishing report rates and how often procedures are followed.

key_terms.definition: Training built for the duties and risks of a specific job, given on top of general awareness.
The process of preparing new staff, including security training before or soon after they get access.

subtopics.name: Social Engineering Tactics
subtopics.definition: Social engineering is manipulating people into giving up information, access or money by exploiting trust, fear, helpfulness or urgency instead of technical flaws.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It is often easier to trick a person than to break a system. One convinced employee can bypass firewalls, encryption and access controls by handing over what the attacker wants.
how_it_works: Attackers research targets using social media, company websites and earlier data leaks.
They build a believable story, such as a new IT contractor, a supplier or an inspector.
They apply pressure: authority, urgency, fear, scarcity, flattery or the wish to help.
They ask for one small step that leads to more: a code, a click, a door held open.
The defense is to slow down, verify through a separate known channel and follow procedure.

types.meaning: Using an invented story and role to win trust and draw out information.
Posing as a real or plausible person, such as a manager, supplier or IT staff member.
Following an authorized person through a secured door without their consent; when they knowingly hold it open, it is often called piggybacking.
Leaving a tempting item, such as a USB drive labeled "salaries", for someone to pick up and use.
Offering a favor, such as free tech help, in exchange for access or information.
Watching someone type a password or read sensitive data on screen.

subtopics.example: A caller tells a school receptionist they are from the district's IT supplier, the email system will shut down within the hour, and they need the principal's login to save it. The receptionist feels the pressure but remembers the policy that no one shares passwords. They take the caller's name, hang up, ring the IT desk on the number in the staff directory and report the call.

review: Verify unusual requests through a known number or in person
Confirm who is asking before sharing any information
Report the attempt even when you refused it
evidence: Official contact list used for call-backs
Report record with the time, caller details and request made
Visitor and badge logs for in-person attempts
audit_focus.recommend: Report every suspected social engineering attempt to the security team, including the ones you stopped.
audit_focus.decides: The security team decides whether to warn other staff

subtopics.isaca_rule: Pressure is the signal. When a request is urgent, unusual or comes with authority attached, slow down and verify through a channel you already trust, not one the requester supplies. Policy and procedure win over helpfulness, and every attempt should be reported.

exam_traps.trap: The caller knew the manager's name and the project, so the request is genuine.
exam_traps.why: Attackers gather such details from public sources and earlier contacts. Knowing internal facts proves research, not identity, so verify through a known channel.

exam_traps.trap: Verify a caller by calling back the number they give you.
exam_traps.why: The attacker controls that number. Call back on a number from the staff directory or official website, which the attacker can't change.

key_terms.definition: Confirming a request through a separate, trusted channel, such as a known phone number, instead of replying to it.
A way of rushing or scaring the target, such as a deadline, a threat or a claim of authority.
Information gathered from public sources, such as social media and company websites, often used to make a story convincing.

subtopics.name: Phishing and Its Variants
subtopics.definition: Phishing is a message, usually an email, text or call, that pretends to come from a trusted source to trick the reader into clicking, sharing data or paying.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Phishing is one of the most common ways attackers get a first foothold, steal passwords and trigger fraudulent payments. Spotting and reporting it quickly protects the person and the whole organization.
how_it_works: Lures copy trusted senders: a bank, a delivery firm, an executive or the IT team.
Warning signs include urgency, unexpected attachments, requests for passwords or payment, and sender or link addresses that don't match.
Hover over links to see where they really go, and type known addresses yourself instead of clicking.
Report suspected phishing with the approved button or address, and don't forward it to colleagues.
If you clicked or entered a password, report at once; speed limits the damage.

types.meaning: Targets a specific person or team, using personal details to look genuine.
Spear phishing aimed at senior executives or other high-value people.
Uses a real or faked business email account to request payments or changes to bank details.
Phishing by SMS text message.
Phishing by voice call, including recorded or artificially generated voices.
Phishing through a QR code that leads to a fake website.

subtopics.example: A logistics clerk gets an email that looks like it comes from the company's delivery software, warning that their account will lock today unless they sign in through a link. The sender's address is slightly misspelled. The clerk doesn't click, and doesn't forward it to coworkers to ask. They use the report button, then open the real software from their bookmarks to check their account.

review: Inspect the sender address and link destination before acting
Report the message through the approved button or mailbox
Tell the security team at once if you clicked or signed in
evidence: Message headers showing the real sending address
Phishing report record with the time it was sent
Sign-in history for the account that received the message
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected phishing to the security team and leave decisions to block or remove it to them.
audit_focus.decides: The security team decides whether to remove the message company-wide

subtopics.isaca_rule: Don't click, don't reply, report. When a stem shows a suspicious message, the best answer is the approved reporting channel, not deleting it quietly or warning colleagues by forwarding it. If someone already clicked, the answer is to report immediately, not to wait and see.

exam_traps.trap: Delete a suspicious email so no one else clicks it.
exam_traps.why: Deleting it hides the attack from the security team, who may need to block the sender and remove the same message from other inboxes. Report it first.

exam_traps.trap: The email has the company logo and the right name, so it is safe.
exam_traps.why: Logos and names are easy to copy. Check the sender address, the link destination and whether the request itself makes sense.

key_terms.definition: Faking the sender details of a message so it appears to come from someone else.
Collecting usernames and passwords through a fake sign-in page.
An email tool that sends a suspected phishing message straight to the security team for review.

subtopics.name: AI-Boosted Phishing and Deepfakes
subtopics.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) boosted social engineering uses AI tools to write convincing messages, clone voices or fake video, making scams more personal and more plentiful.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Old warning signs such as poor grammar are fading. Attackers can copy an executive's writing style or voice quickly, so people must rely on verification procedures, not on how genuine something looks or sounds.
how_it_works: Generative AI writes fluent, personalized lures in many languages, at large scale.
Voice cloning can copy a person's voice from a short public recording.
Deepfake video can put a familiar face on a live call.
Defenses rely on process: call-backs to known numbers, agreed code phrases and dual approval for payments.
Awareness content is updated with real AI examples and stresses verifying requests, not judging polish.
subtopics.example: A finance officer at a charity joins a video call where the chief executive, looking and sounding normal, asks for an urgent transfer to a new supplier before a deadline. Policy requires two approvers and a call-back for any new payee. The officer pauses, rings the chief executive on their known mobile number and learns they are on leave. The officer then reports the call to the security team.

review: Verify payment or access requests by calling a known number
Confirm a second approver signed off on any new payee
Report suspected deepfakes even when no money was lost
evidence: Call-back record with the number used and the outcome
Payment approval history showing both approvers
Recording or screenshot of the suspicious call or message
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected AI-generated scams to the security team so training and warnings can be updated.
audit_focus.decides: Finance management sets payment approval and call-back rules

subtopics.isaca_rule: If sight and sound can be faked, procedure is the safeguard. Verify high-risk requests, especially for money, passwords and access, through a separate known channel, whoever seems to be asking. Updated training should build this habit rather than teach people to hunt for typos.

exam_traps.trap: The message has perfect grammar and the right tone, so it isn't phishing.
exam_traps.why: AI tools remove the spelling and grammar errors people were taught to look for. Judge the request and verify it, not the quality of the writing.

exam_traps.trap: You saw the executive on video, so the payment request is genuine.
exam_traps.why: Deepfake video and voice can imitate real people on live calls. A call-back on a known number and the normal approval steps are still required.

key_terms.definition: AI-generated or AI-altered audio or video that convincingly imitates a real person.
Using AI to copy a person's voice from recordings so it can say new things.
A control where two authorized people must approve an action, such as a payment, before it happens.
A pre-agreed word or phrase used to confirm identity during unusual or urgent requests.

subtopics.name: Password and Passphrase Protection
subtopics.definition: Password protection means choosing long, unique secrets, storing them safely and adding a second factor, so a stolen or guessed password alone can't unlock an account.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Reused and guessable passwords are a leading cause of account takeover. After one site is breached, attackers try the stolen passwords elsewhere.
how_it_works: Length beats complexity: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (2025) has systems require at least 15 characters when a password is the only factor.
A passphrase of several random words is long, easier to remember and hard to guess.
Use a different password for every account; a password manager makes this practical.
Change a password when there is evidence of compromise, not on a fixed calendar.
New passwords are checked against lists of common and breached ones.
Turn on multifactor authentication (MFA), ideally phishing-resistant kinds such as passkeys or security keys.

rows.label: Length
cells: At least 15 when the password is the only factor; at least 8 when it is one part of MFA

rows.label: Complexity
cells: Must mix upper case, lower case, numbers and symbols
No forced mix; any characters, spaces included

rows.label: Changes
cells: Only when there is evidence of compromise

rows.label: Storage
cells: Memorize it; never write it down

subtopics.example: A volunteer coordinator at a youth sports league uses the same password for the league's email and a personal shopping account. When the shopping site is breached, attackers sign in to the league email and message parents. The league's IT volunteer reports the incident to the board and helps the coordinator set up a password manager, unique passphrases and app-based MFA.

review: Fix any work account the manager flags as reused
Turn on the strongest MFA option each system offers
Report any request to share or reveal a password
evidence: Password manager report flagging reused or weak passwords
MFA enrollment status for your accounts
Breach alerts or blocklist rejection notices
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected password exposure to the security team at once and change the password as they direct.
audit_focus.decides: Security management sets the password and MFA policy

subtopics.isaca_rule: Long, unique and backed by MFA. When a stem compares password rules, pick length, uniqueness, breach checks and MFA over forced complexity or scheduled changes. A password manager is a safeguard, not a risk. Never share a password, even with IT or a manager.

exam_traps.trap: Forcing a password change every 30 days makes accounts safer.
exam_traps.why: Forced changes push people toward predictable tweaks, such as Spring2026! becoming Summer2026!. NIST now says to change on evidence of compromise.

exam_traps.trap: A short password with symbols is stronger than a long passphrase.
exam_traps.why: Length adds far more guessing work than a few symbols, and people use symbols predictably. A long passphrase is stronger and easier to remember.

key_terms.definition: A password made of several words, long enough to resist guessing yet easy to remember.
An app that creates, stores and fills strong, unique passwords, protected by one main secret.
Trying usernames and passwords stolen in one breach on many other sites.
Signing in with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password plus a security key.

subtopics.name: Reporting Culture and Phishing Simulations
subtopics.definition: A reporting culture makes it quick and safe for anyone to report suspicious messages, mistakes or incidents, and phishing simulations let staff practice spotting lures safely.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Security teams can act only on what they know. A fast report, even of one's own mistake, can stop an attack before it spreads; silence lets it grow.
how_it_works: Give people one simple way to report: a button, an email address or a phone number.
Thank reporters and tell them the outcome, so reporting becomes a habit.
Report your own mistakes immediately; delay does more harm than the mistake.
Simulations send realistic, harmless test lures and treat a click as a teaching moment, not grounds for punishment.
Simulations are approved in advance and avoid lures that cause real distress, such as fake bonuses or layoff notices.
Track how many people report and how fast, not just how many click.
subtopics.example: A library assistant clicks a link in an email about overdue fines and only then notices the odd web address. Embarrassed, they consider saying nothing. Remembering that policy promises no blame for honest mistakes, they use the report button within minutes and call the IT help desk, so the security team can reset the password and block the site before anyone else signs in.

review: Flag anything odd at once, including your own slips
Confirm a simulation has written approval before it is sent
Share results by team, never by named individual
evidence: Report records showing time from arrival to first report
Signed approval for each simulation campaign
Simulation results by team: report rate and click rate
audit_focus.recommend: Send simulation results to the awareness lead by team, without naming or shaming individuals.
audit_focus.decides: Management approves simulation campaigns and how results are used

subtopics.isaca_rule: Report early, report always, including your own mistakes. When a stem asks what a user should do after clicking a suspicious link, the answer is to report it immediately through the approved channel. A growing report rate is a sign of a healthy culture.

exam_traps.trap: After clicking a phishing link, close the browser and wait to see if anything happens.
exam_traps.why: Attackers act quickly once they have a foothold or a password, and waiting gives them time. Reporting at once lets the team reset accounts and block the threat.

exam_traps.trap: A falling click rate is the only sign of a successful phishing program.
exam_traps.why: Click rates move with how hard the test lure is. Report rate and time to report show whether people take the right action, which stops real attacks.

key_terms.definition: An authorized fake phishing message sent to staff to practice spotting and reporting it.
The share of people who report a simulated or real phishing message.
How long after a message arrives the first person reports it.

topics.overview: Leaders can't steer security they can't see. This topic covers turning raw measurements into useful metrics, telling performance indicators from key risk indicators (KRIs), setting thresholds that trigger action, and presenting results through dashboards, scorecards and reports, including indicators for AI systems.
can_do: Tell a measure from a metric, and a key performance indicator (KPI) from a key risk indicator (KRI)
Classify a measure as implementation, effectiveness, efficiency or impact
Choose a dashboard, scorecard or report for a given audience and purpose
Name useful AI risk indicators, such as model accuracy, override rates and unapproved AI tool use

subtopics.name: Measures and Metrics: The Basics
subtopics.definition: A measure is a raw, quantified result, such as 940 of 1,000 laptops patched; a metric compares measures against a goal to show progress or risk.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without measurement, leaders fund security on instinct and can't tell whether it works. Good metrics show what is improving, what is slipping and where to act next.
how_it_works: Start from a goal, such as patching critical flaws quickly, then pick measures that show progress toward it.
Good measures are objective, accurate, repeatable and comparable over time.
Collect data the same way every period, so trends mean something.
A baseline is the starting value; a target is where the goal says you should be.
A few meaningful metrics beat many that no one acts on.
Every metric should lead to a decision or action; if it doesn't, drop it.
subtopics.example: A city council's IT team reports "12,000 threats blocked this month" to councilors, who can't tell whether that is good. The security lead replaces it with "critical patches applied within 14 days: 78%, target 95%". A junior analyst who pulls the patch data each month uses the same query and cutoff date every time, so the trend stays comparable.

review: Confirm each metric you report has a goal and a target
Keep collection steps identical from one period to the next
Note any change in collection method, with the date
evidence: Saved query or script used to pull the data
Metric definition sheet with goal, target and owner
Past values showing the trend over time
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the metric owner before changing a definition, and flag numbers that drive no decision.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses which metrics to track and sets their targets

subtopics.isaca_rule: A useful metric ties to a goal, has a target and changes a decision. Raw counts such as "attacks blocked" rarely do. When a stem asks for the BEST metric, pick the one that shows progress against an objective, collected consistently, over a big number with no context.

exam_traps.trap: More blocked attacks this month means security is improving.
exam_traps.why: Blocked-attack counts mostly reflect how many attackers tried. They say little about whether controls work or risk is falling, which makes them a vanity metric.

exam_traps.trap: Switch to a better data source whenever one appears, without noting it.
exam_traps.why: Changing the method quietly breaks the trend. If the method must change, record it and restate the baseline so comparisons stay honest.

key_terms.definition: A quantified result, such as a count or percentage, before it is compared with a goal.
A measure compared with a goal or target, used to track progress and support decisions.
The starting value of a measure, used to judge later change.
A number that looks impressive but does not inform a decision or show real progress.

subtopics.name: Types of Security Measures
subtopics.definition: Security measures fall into types by what they show: whether controls exist, whether they work, how fast they work and what they mean for the business.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Knowing the type prevents a common mistake: reporting that a control exists as proof that it works. Executives need impact measures; operators need implementation and efficiency measures to run controls day to day.
how_it_works: NIST SP 800-55 Volume 1 (2024) sorts measures into four types: implementation, effectiveness, efficiency and impact.
Programs usually start with implementation measures, then add the other types as data matures.
Leading indicators look ahead to growing risk; lagging indicators record what has already happened.
Time-based metrics such as mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to recover (MTTR) track efficiency.
Impact measures translate security results into money, mission and trust for leaders.

types.meaning: Shows whether a control is in place, often as a percentage. Example: share of laptops with disk encryption.
Shows whether a control achieves its intended result. Example: share of simulated phishing emails that staff report.
Shows how quickly controls give feedback or problems are fixed. Example: average days to patch critical flaws.
Shows the effect on the mission or finances. Example: cost of security incidents this year.

subtopics.example: A clinic's security report says "100% of staff completed phishing training". The practice manager asks whether phishing is actually being stopped. A junior analyst explains that completion is an implementation measure and adds two more for the next report: the share of test phishing emails staff report, an effectiveness measure, and the average time to report, an efficiency measure.

review: Label each reported measure as implementation, effectiveness, efficiency or impact
Confirm effectiveness claims rest on outcome data, not completion counts
Compare time-based metrics with their targets each period
evidence: Ticket timestamps used to calculate detection and recovery times
Simulation and incident data behind effectiveness figures
Metric catalog listing each measure's type and owner
audit_focus.recommend: Point out to the report owner any claim of effectiveness backed only by implementation data.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides which measures appear in executive reports

subtopics.isaca_rule: Existence isn't effectiveness. When a stem asks whether a control is working, pick an effectiveness measure over one that only proves the control exists. For executives, translate results into impact on the mission and finances.

exam_traps.trap: 100% training completion shows the awareness program is effective.
exam_traps.why: Completion is an implementation measure: it shows the control is in place. Effectiveness asks whether behavior changed, such as more phishing reports and fewer successful lures.

exam_traps.trap: MTTR measures how often systems fail.
exam_traps.why: Mean time to recover measures how long recovery takes on average. How often systems fail is tracked by mean time between failures (MTBF).

key_terms.definition: A metric that signals rising risk before an incident, such as a growing backlog of unpatched systems.
A metric that records outcomes after the fact, such as the number of incidents last quarter.
The average time a problem exists before it is found.
The average time to restore service after a failure or incident; some sources use MTTR for mean time to repair.

subtopics.name: Key Performance and Key Risk Indicators
subtopics.definition: A key performance indicator (KPI) shows how well a process meets its goal; a key risk indicator (KRI) gives early warning that a risk is growing toward its limit.
subtopics.why_it_matters: KPIs tell leaders whether security work is on track; KRIs tell them whether exposure is growing before it becomes an incident. A program needs both, and mixing them up hides warnings.
how_it_works: KPIs look at performance, such as the share of patches applied on time.
KRIs look at exposure, such as internet-facing systems with critical flaws or active accounts of staff who have left.
Good KRIs are leading, measurable and tied to a specific risk in the risk register.
Each KRI has thresholds linked to the organization's risk appetite and tolerance.
The same number can serve as either; what matters is whether it is used to judge performance or to warn of risk.

rows.label: Example
cells: 95% of critical patches applied within 14 days
Critical flaws open more than 30 days on internet-facing servers

subtopics.example: A logistics company tracks how many supplier accounts are reviewed each quarter, a KPI that has been green all year. A junior analyst notices a different number climbing: supplier accounts with administrator rights and no sign-in for 90 days. They suggest it as a KRI for the risk of misused supplier access and send the trend to the risk owner.

review: Confirm each KRI links to a named risk in the register
Compare this period's KRI values with the last to spot upward trends
Report a worsening KRI to the risk owner before it breaches
evidence: KRI history with dates, values and thresholds
Risk register entry the KRI supports
Source system report behind each KRI value
audit_focus.recommend: Send worsening KRI trends to the risk owner with the source data, even before any threshold is crossed.
audit_focus.decides: The risk owner decides how to respond to a worsening KRI

subtopics.isaca_rule: KPIs show performance; KRIs warn of risk. When a stem asks what gives EARLY warning, pick a leading KRI tied to a named risk and tolerance, not a count of past incidents. A green KPI doesn't mean the risk behind it is under control.

exam_traps.trap: Last quarter's incident count is a good early-warning KRI.
exam_traps.why: Incident counts are lagging: they record harm already done. An early-warning KRI tracks conditions that come before incidents, such as unpatched exposure or stale privileged accounts.

exam_traps.trap: If every KPI is green, risk is under control.
exam_traps.why: KPIs measure whether processes run as planned. A process can perform well while exposure grows elsewhere, which is why KRIs are tracked separately.

key_terms.definition: How open an asset or process is to a threat, such as an unpatched system facing the internet.
An account with administrator-level rights that could do serious harm if misused.

subtopics.name: Thresholds, Targets and Escalation
subtopics.definition: Thresholds are preset values on a metric that trigger set actions, such as review or escalation, when crossed; targets are the values the organization aims for.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A metric without a threshold relies on someone happening to notice a problem. Agreed thresholds make escalation automatic and fair, so bad news reaches the right person on time.
how_it_works: Thresholds come from the risk appetite and tolerance agreed by leadership.
Many organizations use color bands to show how close a metric is to its limit.
Each band names an action and an owner, such as amber to the risk owner and red to senior management.
Escalation rules say how fast to report and to whom, and they apply even when the news is awkward.
Thresholds are reviewed when the appetite, the business or the threat picture changes.

types.meaning: Within tolerance; keep monitoring as usual.
Approaching the limit; the risk owner reviews it and plans action.
Beyond tolerance; escalate to senior management to treat or formally accept the risk.

subtopics.example: A school district sets a key risk indicator (KRI) for laptops missing security updates: green under 3%, amber from 3 to 8%, red above 8%. After an update tool fails, the figure jumps to 11% the week before exams. The IT technician who runs the weekly report doesn't wait for the monthly meeting. They follow the red-band rule and alert the IT director that afternoon, attaching the device list.

review: Compare each new value with its threshold bands
Escalate red results without delay through the named path
Confirm any threshold change has a recorded approver and reason
evidence: Threshold table with bands, owners and required actions
Escalation emails or tickets showing when they were sent
Approval records for any threshold change
audit_focus.recommend: Escalate breaches to the named owner as the rule requires, and never change a threshold yourself.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management approves each threshold band and any change to it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Thresholds turn numbers into action. When a metric crosses a threshold, follow the escalation rule at once and send it to the named owner; don't sit on bad news, move the threshold or adjust the number. Leadership sets thresholds, based on risk appetite.

exam_traps.trap: Raise the threshold after a breach so the KRI goes back to green.
exam_traps.why: Moving the line hides the risk without reducing it. Thresholds change only through a deliberate decision by the people who own risk appetite, with a recorded reason.

exam_traps.trap: Wait for the next scheduled report before escalating a red KRI.
exam_traps.why: Escalation rules exist so serious changes reach decision makers quickly. Holding a red result for a routine meeting delays action when it matters most.

key_terms.definition: A preset value on a metric that, once crossed, triggers a defined action.
Passing an issue to a higher authority or the right owner, using a set path and timing.

subtopics.name: Dashboards, Scorecards and Reports
subtopics.definition: Dashboards, scorecards and reports are ways to present metrics: a live visual view, a periodic grade against targets and a written account with context and recommendations.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The right numbers in the wrong format still fail. A board needs a short view of risk and trends, while an operations team needs live detail; mismatched formats bury what matters.
how_it_works: Know the audience first: the board, senior management, risk owners or technical teams.
Dashboards suit people who act daily; they refresh often and let users drill into detail.
Scorecards suit periodic reviews; they compare results with targets, often in green, amber and red.
Reports suit decisions and oversight; they explain trends, causes, risks and the decisions needed.
Show trends over time, not single snapshots, and say what action is needed.
Use the same definitions in all three, so numbers agree wherever they appear.

rows.label: Best for
cells: Operations teams watching day to day
Leaders making decisions or providing oversight

subtopics.example: A hospital's security team shows the board its 40-chart operations dashboard every quarter, and board members lose interest. The security manager replaces it with a one-page scorecard of six metrics against targets and a short report on the two risks needing a decision. A junior analyst preparing the scorecard writes one plain sentence under each red item explaining what it means for patient care.

review: Confirm the same metric shows the same value in every view
Compare the level of detail with what the audience needs
Add a plain-language note explaining each red or amber item
evidence: Metric definitions shared by the dashboard, scorecard and report
Data refresh timestamps on dashboard views
Board or committee feedback on past reports
audit_focus.recommend: Flag numbers that differ between the dashboard and the report to the reporting owner before release.
audit_focus.decides: The security leader decides what is reported to the board

subtopics.isaca_rule: Fit the format to the audience and the decision. Boards and executives get short scorecards and reports on risk, trends and decisions needed; operations teams get live dashboards. When a stem asks how to report to the board, pick concise, business-focused reporting over raw technical detail.

exam_traps.trap: Give the board the full technical dashboard so nothing is hidden.
exam_traps.why: Too much detail hides the few things that need board attention. Boards need summarized risk, trends against appetite and clear decisions, with detail available on request.

exam_traps.trap: A dashboard that is all green means there is nothing to report.
exam_traps.why: Green only means what is measured is within thresholds. Reports still need context: new risks, areas not yet measured and trends heading toward a limit.

key_terms.definition: A scorecard that tracks goals from several viewpoints, such as financial, customer, process and learning, not just one.
Opening a dashboard figure to see the detailed data behind it.

subtopics.name: Using Measurement to Improve
subtopics.definition: Using measurement to improve means acting on what metrics show: finding causes, fixing them, checking the result and refining the metrics themselves over time.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Measuring without acting just documents decline. Metrics earn their cost only when they drive fixes and prove whether those fixes worked.
how_it_works: Look at trends and patterns, not one month in isolation.
Ask why a number moved before deciding what to do about it.
Give each improvement action an owner and a due date.
Measure again to confirm the action worked.
Watch for gaming: once a number becomes a target, people may improve the number instead of the outcome.
Retire metrics no one uses, and add ones for new risks such as artificial intelligence (AI) use.
subtopics.example: A software company's metric for closing vulnerability tickets within 30 days jumps from 60% to 98% in one month. Instead of celebrating, a junior analyst samples ten closed tickets and finds six closed as accepted risk with no owner's approval. They send the sample to the security manager, who changes the rule so only risk owners can close tickets that way.

review: Sample a few records behind any sudden jump or drop
Track each fix in the action log until it closes
Compare the next period's figure with the pre-fix value
evidence: Sampled records compared with the reported figure
Action log with owners, due dates and status
Before-and-after values for the changed metric
audit_focus.recommend: Report suspected metric gaming or poor data quality to the security manager with the sampled evidence.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides improvement priorities and funds the actions

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat a sudden improvement with the same curiosity as a sudden drop. Check the data behind a metric before trusting it, look for causes and confirm fixes with fresh measurement. Gaming a metric is a governance problem to report, not a success.

exam_traps.trap: A metric that hits its target proves the risk is handled.
exam_traps.why: Targets can be met by gaming or by measuring the wrong thing. Confirm that the outcome behind the number improved, for example by sampling the records.

exam_traps.trap: Keep every metric forever so the history is complete.
exam_traps.why: Metrics that no longer drive decisions waste effort and clutter reports. Retire them on purpose and keep their history, while adding metrics for new risks.

key_terms.definition: Changing behavior to improve a number without improving the result it is meant to show.
How accurate, complete, timely and consistent the data behind a metric is.
The underlying reason a problem happened, which a fix must address to stop it recurring.
A repeating cycle of measuring, acting and checking results to get better over time.

subtopics.name: AI Risk Indicators
subtopics.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) risk indicators are metrics that warn when an AI system's accuracy, data, use or availability is moving toward unacceptable risk.
subtopics.why_it_matters: AI systems can fail quietly: accuracy slips, input data changes or staff turn to unapproved tools. Tracking AI-specific key risk indicators (KRIs) on dashboards gives owners time to act before a critical service is disrupted.
how_it_works: Accuracy against a held-back test set, tracked over time, signals model drift.
Comparing current input data with the data the model learned from can warn earlier than accuracy alone.
The human override rate shows how often staff reject the AI's output; a rise suggests declining quality.
Use of unapproved AI tools and attempts to send sensitive data to AI services show policy risk.
Availability and response times of AI services, including outside providers, show continuity risk.
Each AI KRI has an owner, thresholds and an escalation path, like any other KRI.
subtopics.example: An insurance firm uses an AI tool to flag suspicious claims. Its dashboard shows claim handlers overriding the tool's low-risk rating on 4% of claims in spring and 15% by autumn. A junior analyst sees the override rate cross the amber threshold and reports it to the model owner, who finds the model had not learned a new fraud pattern.

review: Compare AI accuracy and override rates with their thresholds
Confirm each AI KRI maps to an entry in the AI inventory
Report threshold crossings to the model owner with the trend
evidence: Dashboard history of accuracy, drift and override rates
Named contacts for each model, with deputies
Web proxy blocks for AI sites outside the approved list
audit_focus.recommend: Report AI KRI breaches to the model owner and the risk owner as the escalation path requires.
audit_focus.decides: The model owner decides whether to retrain, roll back or pause

subtopics.isaca_rule: Measure AI like any critical risk: pick leading indicators, tie them to the AI inventory and the model owner, set thresholds and escalate. A model can look healthy on uptime while drifting on accuracy, so track both performance and availability.

exam_traps.trap: AI service uptime of 99.9% shows the AI risk is low.
exam_traps.why: Uptime shows the service answers, not that its answers are right. Accuracy, drift and override rates show whether the AI still does its job.

exam_traps.trap: AI risk indicators are only for data scientists.
exam_traps.why: AI KRIs belong in the same dashboards and reports as other risks, with owners and thresholds. Leaders need to see them, not just technical staff.

key_terms.definition: A change in the input data an AI system receives compared with the data it learned from.
How often people reject or change an AI system's output; a rising rate can signal declining quality.
Data held back from training and used to check an AI model's accuracy.

key_terminologies.Governance, risk and compliance (GRC): A joined-up way of directing an organization, managing its risks and meeting its obligations.
key_terminologies.Risk appetite: The amount and type of risk leaders are willing to take to pursue their goals.
key_terminologies.Data owner: The business leader accountable for a data set, who decides its classification and who may access it.
key_terminologies.Custodian: The person or team, often IT, that looks after data or systems as the owner directs.
key_terminologies.Framework: A published structure of practices or controls that organizes security work, such as NIST CSF 2.0.
key_terminologies.Compliance: Meeting the laws, regulations, contracts and internal policies that apply, and being able to prove it.
key_terminologies.Redundancy: Spare components or paths that take over when one fails.
key_terminologies.High availability (HA): Keeping a service running with very little downtime, using redundancy and failover.
key_terminologies.Business continuity (BC): Keeping critical business functions running during and after a disruption.
key_terminologies.Disaster recovery (DR): Restoring the technology and data that business functions depend on.
key_terminologies.Business impact analysis (BIA): A study of critical functions, their dependencies and how harm grows over time when they stop.
key_terminologies.Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD): The longest a function can be down before harm becomes unacceptable.
key_terminologies.Recovery time objective (RTO): The target time to restore a function; it must fit within the MTD.
key_terminologies.Recovery point objective (RPO): The most data, measured in time, the business can afford to lose.
key_terminologies.Hot site: A recovery site with equipment, connections and current data, ready within minutes to hours.
key_terminologies.Cold site: A recovery site with space, power and cooling only; equipping it takes days to weeks.
key_terminologies.Immutable backup: A backup that can't be changed or deleted until its retention period ends.
key_terminologies.Model drift: A gradual decline in an AI model's accuracy as real-world conditions change.
key_terminologies.Security culture: The shared attitudes and habits that shape how people treat security every day.
key_terminologies.Social engineering: Manipulating people, instead of systems, to gain information, access or money.
key_terminologies.Phishing: A fake message that pretends to come from a trusted source to trick the reader.
key_terminologies.Deepfake: AI-generated or AI-altered audio or video that imitates a real person.
key_terminologies.Passphrase: A long password made of several words, easier to remember and hard to guess.
key_terminologies.Multifactor authentication (MFA): Signing in with two or more different kinds of proof.
key_terminologies.Metric: A measure compared with a goal or target to show progress or risk.
key_terminologies.Key performance indicator (KPI): A metric showing how well a process meets its goal.
key_terminologies.Key risk indicator (KRI): A metric giving early warning that a risk is growing toward its limit.
key_terminologies.Dashboard: A visual, frequently updated view of metrics for people who act on them daily.
key_terminologies.Scorecard: A periodic summary of results against targets, often color-coded.
